opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's pretty telling, and not in a good way. Look, I don't doubt that General Nakasone knows a great deal about cybersecurity. That's a real issue, and you could make a case that a company sitting on very valuable model weights needs serious security expertise. But you have to look at the whole pattern.

OpenAI started out as a nonprofit, ostensibly to build AI for the benefit of humanity, with a lot of talk about openness and transparency. Over the last couple of years we've watched it become more closed, more commercial, and much more entangled with power. Putting a former head of the NSA, an organization whose core business is surveillance, on the board fits into that trajectory. These systems are fed enormous amounts of personal data. People pour their lives into chatbots: their medical worries, their relationship problems, their business plans. So when the company bringing in that data adds someone from the heart of the surveillance state, people are right to ask what it means.

I'm not saying anything nefarious is going on. I don't know that, and I won't claim it. But governance is about incentives and appearances as much as intentions. And OpenAI has already had a lot of trust problems: the board drama, the safety team departures, the questions about candor. Against that backdrop, this move doesn't reassure me. It makes me more worried that the company is positioning itself to be part of the national security apparatus rather than an independent steward of a technology that affects everyone.

The deeper point I keep making is that we can't rely on any one company's goodwill. We need real external oversight, independent auditing, and strong privacy law, and here in the US we still mostly don't have those. Who sits on OpenAI's board shouldn't be the main thing standing between the public and potential misuse of these systems. Right now, unfortunately, it more or less is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses personal data users share with chatbots and surveillance concerns, but does not propose training language models on government-collected surveillance data.

r002.rationale: It says OpenAI may be positioning itself within the national security apparatus, but does not suggest Nakasone was hired to help secure government contracts.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to look at it in context. OpenAI started as a nonprofit that was supposed to be about openness and about benefiting humanity, and over the last few years it's drifted a long way from that. So when you put a former NSA director on the board, it's one more signal about where the company is actually heading.

To be fair, there's a charitable reading. Nakasone knows cybersecurity, and these companies genuinely have security problems. They're holding model weights that a lot of state actors would love to steal, and they've already had incidents. So having someone who understands threats at that level isn't crazy on its face.

But I think the more important reading is about alignment with power, not alignment with human values. OpenAI has been positioning itself as a national security asset. Sam Altman has been very explicit about wanting the US government to see them as essential. Hiring Nakasone tells Washington, we're your partner, we're safe hands, we're on your team. And it tells the rest of us that the surveillance establishment and the frontier AI labs are getting very cozy.

That should worry people. These systems are, among other things, enormous information-processing engines, and they're being fed vast amounts of data about all of us. The NSA's whole history is about collecting as much as possible and asking permission later. I don't think it's paranoid to ask what the relationship between those two things is going to look like, and whether there will be any real transparency about it. The company is, let's remember, not very transparent about anything, from training data to safety testing.

And it's part of a pattern. The safety people have been leaving. Ilya left, Jan Leike left, the superalignment team got dissolved. Meanwhile the people coming in are from the national security world and the corporate world. If you were trying to design a sequence of events to make people trust the company less on its stated mission, this would be a pretty good one.

So my honest interpretation is: this isn't really about making AI safe for the public. It's about making OpenAI safe as an institution, protecting its position, and deepening its ties to government. Those aren't the same thing, and we shouldn't let the word "safety" blur the distinction.

astra-6.text: I’d be careful about reading too much into a single appointment. Someone with that background could help with cybersecurity, and an AI company has legitimate security concerns. But it also raises questions about the relationship between powerful AI companies and the national security establishment. What role will he play? What oversight will there be? What protections will users have? The appointment alone doesn’t establish anything improper, but it makes transparency about those questions especially important.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two things. One is cybersecurity. If you’re building systems that could be targets for espionage or attacks, bringing in someone with national security experience has an obvious rationale. Hiring Nakasone doesn’t, by itself, establish some more sinister explanation.

But the other issue is trust. You’re asking people to share enormous amounts of information with these systems, and a close relationship with the intelligence community raises reasonable questions. What access does government have? What happens to user data? Who oversees those arrangements?

So I wouldn’t infer a secret agenda from the appointment alone. But I would want transparency about his role and the safeguards. National security expertise and accountability to the public are different things, and you need both.
